entries.title: Chinatown and Bridgeport residents press Amtrak leaders to 'pump the breaks' on rail yard plan
entries.summary: <p>Amtrak officials and developers faced off against angry community members Thursday, opposing construction plans for a massive rail yard in Chinatown, Bridgeport and Armour Square beginning as early as the end of this year.</p><p>The plan, headed by White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" >Justin Ishbia’s</a> company, Canal Edge LLC, includes a proposal for the Sox to play at a mixed-use facility along the Chicago River called The Railyards in the South Loop and Amtrak’s maintenance facility to move into the neighborhood on South Canal Street between West 33rd and 35th streets.</p><p>Hundreds of residents, some dressed in T-shirts that read “Protect our community, stop Amtrak’s rail yard,” flooded the meeting. Tensions rose as Amtrak leaders and developers claimed there were no significant impacts on the environment or quality of life for nearby residents housed near the proposed site.</p><p>Residents responded by questioning the studies Amtrak has done regarding impacts on safety, the environment, noise and other factors. The project has received $600 million and a categorical exclusion from the federal government to bypass certain environmental tests and an environmental impact statement to break ground faster, but residents also questioned that.</p><p>“You’re treating us like we’re idiots. We’re not idiots,” one resident said. “We’re intelligent, hardworking people making our home here.”</p><p>Steven Segerlin, who runs commercial development at Amtrak, said the company needs a new site for a rail yard to replace its current 14th Street facility. The revamped site would allow the company to modernize its maintenance, cleaning and storage practices, allowing for fewer delays.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div He said Segerlin should have started the meeting by asking the panel of Amtrak leaders and developers a question instead of the crowd who ever had their Amtrak train delayed.</p><p>“Ask people up there if they would want this facility next to their house,” Daley said.</p><p>Residents criticized the project due to its location in a residential neighborhood, with more than 6,000 people living within 500 feet of the proposed site, compared to 29 living within the same radius of the current Amtrak maintenance facility, according to Lee. entries.title: Lincoln-Way board votes to allow students involved in racist incident to withdraw instead of being expelled
entries.summary: <p>The Lincoln-Way School District Board of Education voted unanimously to allow the students involved in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/05/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racial-harassment" >racial harassment incident</a> during the football game at Homewood-Flossmoor on Sept. 4 to withdraw voluntarily from Lincoln-Way East rather than be expelled.</p><p>“This investigation, which involved interviewing numerous students, reviewing multiple video recordings and angles, and speaking with their attorneys, took the administration only eight school days and ultimately resulted in the administration recommending expulsion for the students determined to have been involved,” Supt. Scott Tingley said at the school board meeting on Thursday. “The parents of those students have chosen, however, to voluntarily withdraw their children from Lincoln-Way East High School and forfeit all student privileges rather than proceed with the expulsion process.”</p><p>The Lincoln-Way East students were caught on video racially taunting H-F students at a football game in Flossmoor by mimicking monkeys.</p><p>The school board did not name the students or specifically outline the reasons for each student’s discipline. The board returned from closed session and voted to allow six students to withdraw instead of being expelled. Tingley spoke after the vote.</p><p>“My responsibility as superintendent was to ensure the law and the board of education policies were followed at every step with respect to those students’ discipline,” Tingley said. “To do that, the administration conducted a thorough and timely investigation and assessed each student’s individual level of involvement and offered every one of them the right to be heard.”</p><p>The Lincoln-Way school board acknowledged what happened at the football game and released an apology statement the next day. </p><p>Later the same weekend, Homewood-Flossmoor officials accused a Lincoln-Way East girls cross-country coach and team members of racial abuse at a cross country meet in Western Springs.</p><p>H-F provided written statements from three cross-country athletes describing a Lincoln-Way East coach making comments about “running past those monkeys,” and that some of the Lincoln-Way East team began cheering and making “noises that were racist” and “monkey gestures.”</p><p>Lincoln-Way investigated the incident and concluded that “neither its staff nor student athletes intended to harass, intimidate or offend any of their competitors or those competitors’ families.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racist-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >Second racist Lincoln-Way East incident alleged by Homewood-Flossmoor</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/09/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racisim-jennifer-norrell" >After alleged racism, Homewood-Flossmoor weighs future with Lincoln-Way East</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Tingley addressed the cross-country incident at Thursday’s board meeting.</p><p>“The district and certain of its employees have been threatened with legal action, and the allegations surrounding that incident are currently under investigation by the [Illinois High School Association],” Tingley said. “We are fully cooperating with the IHSA and will cooperate with any other appropriate agency or law enforcement authority should an additional investigation occur.</p><p>“While that investigation remains ongoing, I will not make additional public comments regarding the allegations. The district has already made one public statement available noting that it has been unable to corroborate the allegations.</p><p>“Once the IHSA has completed its investigation and it is clear that no additional investigations are pending, I intend to address the matter more fully.”</p><p>The IHSA's Matt Troha told the Sun-Times earlier on Thursday that the action at the Lincoln-Way school board meeting would "provide the IHSA with a better timeline moving forward."<br></p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas, White Sox, don't mind playing from behind: 'We like being the underdog'
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox returned home this week, in second place in the division standings for the first time since beating the Guardians on Independence Day.</p><p>Maybe it’s for the best.</p><p>“We play better when we’re behind,” All-Star third baseman <b>Miguel Vargas</b> told the Sun-Times. “We like being the underdog. We like to go out there when people do not believe in us.”</p><p>Beginning his career with the Dodgers, bouncing between Triple-A and the majors, Vargas has been on hand for a post-clinch locker room celebration in the major leagues before. Now, as the heart and soul of a Sox lineup fighting to stay afloat in the American League Central, he thinks champagne would taste sweeter in the White Sox clubhouse.</p><p>“With the Dodgers, you always expect to go to the World Series every year,” Vargas said. “When you don’t do it, it’s a failure. Here, I feel nobody believes in us. Everyone doubts us. We were supposed to be the 28th team in MLB this year [according to] ESPN. Now we’re on the way to the postseason, and being underdogs is what it’s about. I feel like that’s what makes us better, being underdogs. That’s what’s brought us to this beautiful year we’ve had.”</p><p>Recent weeks have found the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/13/this-is-why-you-play-white-sox-readying-for-all-important-al-central-showdown-in-cleveland-will-venable-davis-martin-sean-burke-colson-montgomery-randal-grichuk" target="_blank" ><u>Sox trying to reclaim the loose clubhouse atmosphere</u></a> they had while defying expectations, like the ones Vargas referenced, with a 50-45 first half mark. Now that a crushing series loss in Cleveland has their division title odds looking shaky again, maybe they should embrace that feeling.</p><p>“We put ourselves in this position, and we need to clean it up,” Vargas said. “We’re going to be there in the playoffs, and kick some ass too.”</p><p><b>Help from the other side</b></p><p>After <b>Sean Burke</b> gave up a career-worst seven runs in just 1 ⅓ innings on Sept. 8 against Pittsburgh, he sought insight from a surprising source: the opposing No. 2 hitter from that night.</p><p>“I work out with <b>Brandon Lowe</b> in the offseason with my agency,” said Burke, who is a Bledsoe Agency client alongside the Pirates infielder. “So I was talking to him a little bit about what he was seeing, how he felt in the box based on prior times he’s faced me.”</p><p>Lowe’s observations that Burke’s pitches were cutting and blending together lined up with what he was already working on. Ahead of recovering for five innings without an earned run allowed on Monday in Cleveland, Burke focused on correcting his stride direction, and restoring the feeling behind the baseball upon release.</p><p>Lowe is a pending free agent, so he had little reason not to help out a friend.</p><p><b>Montgomery is day-to-day</b></p><p>After leaving Wednesday’s game with a left wrist contusion caused by a hit-by-pitch, <b>Colson Montgomery</b> was out of the lineup Thursday. The Sox say Montgomery is day-to-day, but that day is unlikely to be Friday.</p><p>“There’s still a lot of pain involved in him swinging,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>.</p><p><b>Castillo to the bullpen</b></p><p>With his 7.76 ERA in a White Sox uniform and nine games remaining, the team is abandoning the idea of trade-deadline acquisition <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/11/white-sox-starter-luis-castillo-feels-hes-very-very-close-to-righting-ship-after-working-on-mechanics-colson-montgomery-strikeout-record-chase-meidroth-joey-bart-will-venable" target="_blank" ><b><u>Luis Castillo</u></b><u> providing a boost to the rotation</u></a>. Venable said Castillo’s next appearance will be out of the bullpen, and Friday’s scheduled starter <b>David Sandlin </b>is effectively <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/15/a-new-and-improved-david-sandlin-should-have-staying-power-in-white-sox-rotation-noah-schultz-colson-montgomery-will-venable-brian-bannister-jose-urquidy" target="_blank" ><u>taking his spot in the rotation</u></a>.</p>

entries.title: Tim Anderson grateful, at peace in retirement as White Sox honor the two-time All-Star's career
entries.summary: <p>Thursday’s retirement ceremony for<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/10/tim-anderson-retirement-chicago-white-sox-southside-city-connect-uniforms-field-of-dreams-game" target="_blank" ><u> former two-time All-Star Tim Anderson</u></a> felt sudden, even with advanced notice.</p><p>“He feels like the story of why Major League Baseball players try to get what they can get when they can get it, because it happens so fast,” said former Sox announcer Jason Benetti, in town to call the game for the Tigers. “His story is some of the brightest lightning in the largest bottle for a time. And then suddenly it's gone.”</p><p>The highlights of Anderson played on the Rate Field Jumbotron were of pristine video quality. The old Southside City Connect jerseys the team played in triggered a nostalgia for an era where Anderson was the heartbeat of the franchise, but were in use in 2024. Just before Anderson was bathed in applause by a thankful crowd, he was congratulated by Tommy Pham–five years his senior–before the Sox DH continued on to his pregame warmups.</p><p>Reached for comment, former White Sox general manager Rick Hahn recalled an anecdote that feels ancient–Anderson convincing him to approve Team USA playing him at second base, and keying a mercy-rule romp of Canada in the World Baseball Classic–and also was from just three years ago.</p><p>“That was TA,” Hahn told the Sun-Times. “Teams were just better when he was in there and setting the tone, which is something he loved to do.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/mXT6EsnpnPU?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="A Letter to Chicago from Tim Anderson (2026)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>He loved it, but as has been clear since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/10/tim-anderson-retirement-chicago-white-sox-southside-city-connect-uniforms-field-of-dreams-game" target="_blank" ><u>Anderson announced his retirement in an emotional Zoom session last month</u></a>, and even upon his return to Rate Field on Thursday night, it took a lot out of him.</p><p>“I looked at it like if I wasn't nervous, I wasn't ready,” Anderson said Thursday. “That first at-bat, I'm always nervous."</p><p>In Chicago early last season playing for the Angels, Anderson speculated that pushing himself to play through the nagging injuries late in his career also altered the mechanics of a swing that captured the 2019 batting title, and four-straight seasons of a .300 average or better. Others, including former teammates, felt his off-the-field mistakes wounded his once indomitable mindset.</p><p>Anderson felt it all, including the large platform his stardom brought, as an everpresent pressure that his enjoyment of the game stopped being able to out-pace. Just discussing his career prompted him to sweat profusely on his Zoom call in August, and before he addressed reporters in the Sox dugout on Thursday, he asked for a towel with which to dot his brow.</p><p>“I never wanted to be in that spotlight,” Anderson said. "I just wanted to be me, and that happened.”</p><p>Which remains a surreal sentiment for Anderson to express. Earlier this very decade, he felt built for the limelight, even more than he felt built to have a career longer than 991 major league games.</p><p>After Tarik Skubal was traded from the Tigers, Benetti found himself watching old video of Anderson ruining the two-time Cy Young winner’s major league debut; homering in the first at-bat of the game and lining an RBI double the following inning, amid a multi-year run of terrorizing Tiger pitching. Playoff games are what Anderson’s White Sox teams had too little of, especially since he had a career .485 postseason batting average.</p><p>“You could set anything up, and Tim Anderson was going to spike it out,” Benetti said. “He was going to make moments.</p><p>But only now is Anderson truly free to enjoy them. He covered his eyes and hugged his family as a scoreboard video segment of his career came to a close. Before that, he laughed about not having to worry about getting on time for a fastball Thursday night.</p><p>Back in the place where he was once at center stage, Anderson seemed content just to watch, and reflect.</p><p>“It's not what you did for me lately, it's what you did,” Anderson said. "Now, looking back at what I did: pretty cool. Pretty awesome, pretty dope, you know what I mean? It was a whole wave.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Judgment day is coming for Sky coach Tyler Marsh
entries.summary: <p>After a disappointing year, some hard conversations are coming for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a>.</p><p>The big one will be with coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> about whether he’s earned a third season.</p><p>Marsh told the Sun-Times on Thursday he hasn’t yet discussed his job status with general manager <b>Jeff Pagliocca</b> or principal owner <b>Michael Alter</b>, and those conversations will be reserved for the offseason.</p><p>Until then, Marsh is full steam ahead.</p><p>“As long as I’m here I’m gonna give my best for this organization and these players and this city,” he said. "I can’t control what happens beyond that, but it’s never a question of if I want to be.”</p><p>“This is what I worked my whole life for. I haven’t had any handouts. I’ve worked and earned my way into an opportunity. You never know when these opportunities come the first time, or ever, and you don’t want to let them slip away.”</p><p>Should Marsh get the boot? On one hand, the Sky have a 30% win rate during Marsh’s tenure, the roster underperformed relative to its talent this year, and end-of-game management was an issue.</p><p>On the other hand, Marsh clearly improved this season, generally has strong relationships with players, and appears to have installed a viable offensive system.</p><p>But maybe the most important factor has nothing to do with Marsh. It’s whether Alter, Pagliocca and company think they can actually attract someone better. They do have an appealing young core in <b>Rickea Jackson</b>,<b> Sydney Taylor</b> and <b>Kamilla Cardoso</b> to go along with two first-round picks in 2027; maybe that’s enough to convince a top-tier coach to come on board.</p><p>But the organization still doesn’t have the best reputation. Nor do they have an All-Star on the roster or a chance at landing one in the lottery. It’s far from a perfect job.</p><p><b>Easy does it</b></p><p>When discussing how he'll manage rotations to close out the season, Marsh has repeatedly used phrases like "exercising caution,” “not wanting to overload anyone” and “preserving bodies.”</p><p>In other words: don’t expect the Sky to be at full throttle during their final week.</p><p><b>DiJonai Carrington</b> missed Thursday’s game against the Mystics managing her foot injury. <b>Natasha Cloud</b> has not been a full participant at practice and left after the first half (knee), and <b>Azurá Stevens</b> also told the Sun-Times that she and the health staff will be managing her knee.</p><p>The upside is that rookies <b>Gabriela Jaquez</b> and <b>Aicha Coulibaly</b> will get more playing time, which should be the priority at this point. But it also means any hope of Marsh strengthening his case with some upsets in the final week is probably naive.</p><p><b>Thank you, Chicago</b></p><p>Not only have the Mystics excelled ahead of schedule this season, they’re also on track to receive a 2027 lottery pick from the Sky.</p><p>That’s because of the pick swap included in the 2025 trade that brought Ariel Atkins to Chicago.</p><p>“Thank goodness [President of Monumental Basketball] Michael Winger and the folks back in D.C. have positioned us to have a lottery pick,” Mystics coach <b>Sydney Johnson</b> said before the game. “We’ll see what happens.”</p><p>As things stand, the Mystics are projected to receive the No. 3 pick, while the Sky would get No. 10 in return.</p><p>The Mystics also own the Sky's 2028 pick which they got in return for guard <b>Jacy Sheldon.</b></p>

entries.title: Francis W. Parker School's expansion gets first city approval, despite ire from neighbors
entries.summary: <p>The Francis W. Parker School scored a victory in its yearslong battle against some Lincoln Park neighbors over its plan to build a middle school on West Belden Avenue.</p><p>The school, which has been in Lincoln Park for 125 years, received approval Thursday for its expansion from the Chicago Plan Commission. The school also sought approval for new athletic field lights and security cameras. The project is now expected to go before the Committee on Zoning, Landmarks and Building Standards next week, according to the school.</p><p>Parker School said the additional building is needed because it has reached capacity at its current property, 330 W. Webster Ave. The private school teaches pre-K through 12th grade and has 940 students, according to a spokesperson. </p><p>It's proposing tearing down the 15-unit Belden by the Park condos at 335 W. Belden Ave. to build a five-story building, which would include a pedestrian overpass connecting the buildings. The new property would also have a multipurpose room and terraces, along with overflow classroom space. </p><p>Parker, which owns the condo building, pegs construction costs at $39 million.</p><p>The expansion would allow Parker to welcome 125 new students and add 30 permanent staff and faculty jobs to accommodate the growth, Principal Dan Frank told commissioners Thursday. The new students and faculty would gradually be added over the course of seven years.</p><p>“The building in our proposal is crucial to helping us achieve those goals because Parker is at capacity,” Frank said. “The only way to increase our student body and to add jobs is to expand our physical space.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-440000" name="image-440000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a3b305c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2981fa5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/85ee04e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Francis W. Parker School at 330 W. Webster Ave. in Lincoln Park." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/85ee04e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/944a53f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/85ee04e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6487x3641+0+514/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fcc%2F8f%2Fdd6d9dc9452fb77dbdbf12aa57d9%2Fplancom-260918-3-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Francis W. Parker School at 330 W. Webster Ave. in Lincoln Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Parker said it’s been discussing the expansion with neighbors and nearby businesses since 2024, and the school has made concessions to address residents' concerns. </p><p>The pedestrian overpass, accessible on the new building’s third and fourth floors, was narrowed and moved farther east. The school is also relocating rooftop mechanical equipment to the east side of the roof, away from neighbors on the building's west side.</p><p>The building’s southwest corner was also cut back to create more natural light for neighboring townhomes, the development team said. And the nearby building at 317-25 W. Belden Ave., owned by Parker, will be kept as residential for the next 30 years, in response to neighborhood concerns over the loss of homes.</p><p>But neighbors still showed up in full force Thursday, with more than 40 people signed up to speak about the proposal. </p><p>Parents of Parker students, alumni and some board members spoke in favor of the proposal, citing the need to better position Parker for the future. But they were outnumbered by opponents of the project, many of whom were against the demolition of the 1909 vintage courtyard building at 335 W. Belden.</p><p>Preservation Chicago urged the commission to reject Parker’s proposal, citing the inclusion of Belden by the Park in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/26/chicago-stock-courtyard-buildings-wind-up-national-register-historic-places" >courtyard building landmark district</a> the group has pursued for a number of years.</p><p>Some detractors pointed to the <a class="Link" href="https://eastlincolnparkneighbors.net/a-better-proposal" target="_blank" >Better Plan</a>, a proposal created by the group East Lincoln Park Neighbors that calls for a five-story building on Parker’s parking lot and a sixth-story aquatic center, to avoid demolishing residential buildings.</p><p>Michelle Hoppe Villegas, board member of the Mid-North Association, said its board opposes the expansion.</p><p>“We ask that you listen to the overwhelming public opposition to amending the current plan development agreement and ask that you reject the private institution … asking to encroach upon our dense and treasured historic neighborhood,” Hoppe Villegas said. “If allowed, Parker will consume and gut this historic community.”</p><p>East Lincoln Park Neighbors said in a statement that Thursday's "vote reflects a rushed and inadequate review of a proposal with lasting consequences for the neighborhood. Chicago’s planning process should welcome genuine community engagement, require timely disclosure of key information, and ensure that public bodies fully scrutinize major developments before approving them. Today, it fell short on all counts.”</p><p>Anny Gary, member of Parker’s board of trustees, said the school’s proposal is the result of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/5/21/21266563/lincoln-park-condo-owners-francis-parker-school-lawsuit-straw-buyers" >years of dialogue</a>. She said the Better Plan isn’t viable and overestimates the amount of developable land in the parking lot by about 35% to 40%.</p><p>“This Proposal is the product of years of collaboration — with neighbors, community groups, local elected officials, and the Parker community — all working together to shape a plan that benefits not only Parker students, but our community and the city of Chicago as a whole,” a Parker spokesperson said in a statement. “From expanding access and financial assistance for Chicago students to bringing new affordable housing and enhanced safety measures to Lincoln Park, this plan reflects Parker's 125-year commitment to being a responsible, engaged neighbor and civic partner."</p><p>The school expects construction to start no sooner than 2028.</p><p>Separately, the Plan Commission approved the proposal for a 19-unit, mixed-income apartment building at 665 W. Sheridan Road and a Fulton Market high-rise, with more than 400 units.</p><p>Northwestern Memorial Hospital’s proposed hospital tower at 330 E. Erie St. also received its first city approval. The 1.2 million-square-foot tower will create more than 200 new patient beds and employ more than 1,000 workers when complete. It’s estimated to cost $1.5 billion and would be completed in 2031, if approved by the City Council.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2020/5/21/21266563/lincoln-park-condo-owners-francis-parker-school-lawsuit-straw-buyers" >Condo owners allege Francis W. Parker School tried to fraudulently take over their building, call the move ‘morally bankrupt’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Man, 29, shot while sitting in car in Morgan Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was hospitalized Thursday after he was shot in the neck while inside a vehicle in Morgan Park, police said. </p><p>Police said the victim, a 29-year-old man, sustained a single gunshot wound to the neck at about 8 p.m. when someone fired at the vehicle in the 1100 block of West 114th Place. </p><p>The man was reportedly a passenger in the vehicle when the gunman appeared from a nearby alley and fired shots, police said.</p><p>He was transported to Christ Hospital and is listed in good condition, police said. </p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating the shooting.</p>

entries.title: 2 women wounded after being shot in Chatham alley
entries.summary: <p>A 56-year-old woman was wounded after being shot in an alley in Chatham late Thursday, police said.</p><p>At about 8:12 p.m., police said the woman was walking in an alley in the 8100 block of South Maryland Avenue when she reportedly heard a verbal altercation and saw a 23-year-old woman run to the area from a nearby apartment complex, being pursued by a man. The man then pulled a gun and fired several shots at the woman. </p><p>One of the rounds hit the 56-year-old woman in the leg. The 23-year-old woman sustained a graze wound to her legs, police said.</p><p>The injured 56-year-old woman was treated at the scene before being transported to the University of Chicago Medical Center in good condition. The other woman refused treatment and was listed in good condition.</p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Woodlawn junior DJ Morgan runs for 261 yards, 4 TDs to beat Bowen
entries.summary: <p>Images of Woodlawn’s DJ Morgan will haunt Bowen’s football players for at least the next few days.</p><p>The Boilermakers were powerless to stop Morgan on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/17/high-school-football-scores-week-5" >Thursday</a>. The junior running back scored four touchdowns and ran for 261 yards in Woodlawn’s 54-6 win against visiting Bowen.</p><p>Morgan’s first carry went 34 yards for a TD. His second carry was a 50-yard TD, and his third went for a 64-yard score. Then he added an 83-yard TD run in the third quarter, which started the running clock.</p><p>“He’s been a premier player since he was a freshman,” Warriors coach Jacob Engleton said. “He has so much heart. Even on defense, he is one of our hardest hitters. He is one of our most willing guys on special teams. He is the personality of this team. DJ means a lot to us.”</p><p>Morgan did all of his damage on just eight carries. He also caught a 28-yard pass from Michael Hickman.</p><p>“I’m smaller, so everyone looks down on me, so I just work,” Morgan said. “I try to get to the end zone every time I get the ball.”</p><p>Hickman threw a 20-yard touchdown pass to Brian Jackson late in the first half, and Jackson also contributed a 32-yard TD run.</p><p>Senior lineman Yamari Crowder dominated on defense for the Warriors. Bowen (2-3, 0-2) managed just 39 rushing yards and eight passing yards.”</p><p>“I didn’t feel like getting blocked today, so I didn’t get blocked,” Crowder said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Woodlawn junior Darryl Morgan has two carries and 2 TDs. The first was 35 yards and this one was 50. <br><br>The Warriors lead Bowen 16-0. <a href="https://t.co/l0X5moOITQ">pic.twitter.com/l0X5moOITQ</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2100712676968014317?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 17, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Woodlawn (4-1, 2-0 White South) went undefeated last season in the Blue Division. The Warriors' only loss in the past two seasons was to Brother Rice in Week 2.</p><p>“Everyone in the Public League knows there is a whole other animal out there when you get to the Catholic League and to the state playoffs,” Engleton said. “We just wanted our guys to see it. The band, the massive numbers, the size difference. So if we are blessed enough to get into the playoffs, it is familiar to us.”</p><p>Engleton said the 69-0 loss to Brother Rice helped his team refocus.</p><p>“We gave it our all, but we saw the level we need to reach,” Woodlawn senior Dale Ellis said. “Those are the big dogs.”</p><p>Woodlawn could qualify for the state playoffs this season. The Warriors have to finish first in the White South or finish second and then defeat a Red Division team in a special playoff game.</p><p>“That has been the goal since the start,” Engleton said. “We have a lot of talent over here. It is a committee. All of our guys are prepared. We make sure everyone gets equal reps, and it just shows on the field.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-890000" name="html-embed-module-890000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports/video/7686709276408122654" data-video-id="7686709276408122654" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports?refer=embed">@michaelsobriensports</a> Woodlawn stars Yamari Crowder, Dale Allen and DJ Morgan speak after beating Bowen. <a title="ihsa" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/ihsa?refer=embed">#ihsa</a> <a title="football" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/football?refer=embed">#football</a> <a title="chicago" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/chicago?refer=embed">#chicago</a> <a title="woodlawn" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/woodlawn?refer=embed">#woodlawn</a> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-7686709347162065695?refer=embed">♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Glen Ellyn man charged with February murder of woman in West Ridge
entries.summary: <p>A man was charged with the murder of a woman in West Ridge in February, police said.</p><p>Darreon Plummer, 33, of suburban Glen Ellyn, faces a first-degree murder charge in connection with the fatal shooting of 36-year-old Da’J Dameka Flowers. Flowers was fatally shot near her home in the 6900 block of North Bell Avenue on Feb. 6.</p><p>Plummer was arrested near O'Hare International Airport Wednesday. He's scheduled to appear in court Friday. </p>
